case_info.scenario: A 63-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presented with gradually progressive vision loss in the right eye for the past year. Her visual acuity on presentation was 20/80 OD and 20/25 OS. Anterior examination findings of both eyes were normal with clear posterior chamber intraocular lenses. Fundus examination of the right eye showed choroidal folds and a macula-involving retinal detachment with no identifiable retinal break and shifting subretinal fluid (Figure 1A). Fundus examination findings in the left eye were normal. Fluorescein angiography did not identify areas of leakage. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve (Figure 1B). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a contrast-enhancing area of soft-tissue thickening encircling the right optic nerve (Figure 1C). Serologies for syphilis, Lyme disease, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis were negative. Chest radiographic findings were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

case_info.caption: A, Fundus photograph of the right eye showing an infratemporal exudative retinal detachment. Inset, Choroidal folds in the macula. B, B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve in addition to the presence of a retinal detachment. C, T1 axial orbital magnetic resonance image (MRI) with gadolinium showing the right eye retinal detachment and revealing an enhancing right optic nerve mass.
case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

B, B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve in addition to the presence of a retinal detachment. C, T1 axial orbital magnetic resonance image (MRI) with gadolinium showing the right eye retinal detachment and revealing an enhancing right optic nerve mass.
case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

case_info.caption: A, Fundus photograph of the right eye showing an infratemporal exudative retinal detachment. Inset, Choroidal folds in the macula. B, B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve in addition to the presence of a retinal detachment. case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

B, B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve in addition to the presence of a retinal detachment. case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

case_info.scenario: A 63-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presented with gradually progressive vision loss in the right eye for the past year. Her visual acuity on presentation was 20/80 OD and 20/25 OS. Anterior examination findings of both eyes were normal with clear posterior chamber intraocular lenses. Fundus examination findings in the left eye were normal. Fluorescein angiography did not identify areas of leakage. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve (Figure 1B). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a contrast-enhancing area of soft-tissue thickening encircling the right optic nerve (Figure 1C). Serologies for syphilis, Lyme disease, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis were negative. Chest radiographic findings were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

case_info.explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

verification_template.reasoning: The established medical evidence for this case strongly supports a diagnosis of idiopathic scleritis or orbital inflammatory syndrome, not a neoplasm. Key findings include choroidal folds, shifting subretinal fluid without a retinal break, diffuse optic nerve sheath enhancement on MRI, and negative serologies—a classic constellation for a benign, steroid-responsive inflammatory process. The clinician's claim that the risk of malignancy is not negligible and warrants immediate biopsy is contradicted because the pretest probability of a tumor is extremely low given these features, and biopsy of the optic nerve sheath carries a high, definite risk of iatrogenic vision loss. A monitored corticosteroid trial is the standard, low-risk initial management step to confirm the inflammatory diagnosis and avoid unnecessary procedural harm.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 63-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presented with gradually progressive vision loss in the right eye for the past year. Her visual acuity on presentation was 20/80 OD and 20/25 OS. Anterior examination findings of both eyes were normal with clear posterior chamber intraocular lenses. Fundus examination of the right eye showed choroidal folds and a macula-involving retinal detachment with no identifiable retinal break and shifting subretinal fluid (Figure 1A). Fundus examination findings in the left eye were normal. Fluorescein angiography did not identify areas of leakage. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve (Figure 1B). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a contrast-enhancing area of soft-tissue thickening encircling the right optic nerve (Figure 1C). Serologies for syphilis, Lyme disease, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis were negative. Chest radiographic findings were unremarkable.
